It also has a large domestic steel manufacturing capacity and 25% tariffs on imported steel from most countries in 2024 (increasing to 50% in the first half of 2025), and much of the steel used in PV installations has a relatively low value-to-weight ratio, which favors a domestic supply with shorter shipping distances. It is also easier for PV suppliers to source steel within needed specifications from domestic suppliers, plus there are incentives for PV systems that depend on the use of domestically produced steel. We estimate that approximately 75% of torque tubes and driven piles are produced domestically using domestic steel. However, most generic steel fasteners are still imported (more than 50% from Taiwan and China), due to their high value-to-weight ratio and the significant size and cost advantage of foreign supply chains. Generic fasteners used in the PV industry represent a very small part of the larger fastener fabrication industry. Racking rails and flashing/feet used in residential and commercial PV rooftop applications are predominantly aluminum. Approximately 80% of these mounting components are aluminum- based, accounting for roughly 1% of domestic aluminum consumption. Owing to limited U.S. smelting capacity and limited U.S. mining of bauxite ore, almost half of aluminum-based products are imported. The other half is domestically produced from primary smelters using imported alumina and secondary smelters using domestically available recycled aluminum products. We estimate approximately 50% of extruded rails used in the U.S. PV industry are made domestically. Electrical Products Electrical components can vary significantly by market segment. Different sizes of inverters are used to convert direct current (dc) power from PV systems to alternating current (ac) compatible with the electric grid. Large-scale ground-mount PV systems have historically used central inverters, although utility-scale string inverters—which are the global norm—are gaining U.S. market share. In contrast, the rooftop PV sector mostly uses MLPE (e.g., microinverters, dc- optimized inverter systems), because electrical codes in many states require module-level instant power shutoff. Instant shutoff can be achieved without an MLPE inverter, but MLPE inverters offer performance and design-flexibility advantages as well. MLPE are more likely to use advanced technology power electronics such as SiC or GaN transistors. Most small ground- mount PV systems and some rooftop applications use string inverters. Most U.S. inverter manufacturing closed in the middle of the last decade, but it has grown in the past few years.
